claims.text: Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling will generate substantial lattice strain and grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi.
The milling-induced strain and grain refinement will lower the activation-energy barrier for an FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
Approximately 6 hours of milling will suppress brittle HCP-phase formation otherwise driven by Ti segregation.
SPS at 1000°C will produce greater than 99% relative density in the milled CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
A high SPS heating rate and short dwell will kinetically retain a refined, strained FCC/BCC solid-solution state without excessive HCP precipitation.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the FCC/BCC/HCP phase stability of the proposed CoCrFeNiTi state.
Milling-induced strain energy shifts thermodynamic equilibrium toward BCC and counteracts the Ti-induced HCP tendency.
The starting elemental Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti powders have particle sizes of 10–50 µm and are equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
The proposed processing conditions are 300–400 RPM milling at a 10:1 ball-to-powder ratio followed by SPS at 1000°C and 50 MPa with a 100°C/min heating rate and a 5–10 minute dwell.
Milling will produce a nanocrystalline grain size below 100 nm and a high dislocation density.
Six hours of milling will produce a dislocation density above 10^14 m^-2.
The critical milling-induced strain shifts the effective VEC threshold for phase stability and lowers the free energy of BCC relative to HCP.
At 1000°C, SPS provides enough atomic mobility for diffusion and porosity elimination while remaining below the threshold for Ti-rich HCP precipitation.
Longer milling can lead to oxide or carbide contamination or precipitation.
The processed alloy will be single-phase or dual-phase FCC/BCC with negligible HCP content.
The processed alloy will exceed 400 HV because of Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening and solid-solution strengthening.
As-cast CoCrFeNiTi typically has coarse grains, hardness below 200 HV, porosity or segregation, and an FCC/HCP phase mixture.
Sintering above 1050°C will permit Ti segregation and HCP precipitation or excessive grain growth.
Milling beyond 10 hours will create excessive oxygen or carbon contamination and stabilize unwanted oxides or carbides.
Vickers testing at 100–200 g can minimize indentation-size effects and isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.
